summary: Adding a Blur to a rectangle used to change nothing at all, and on a circle the soft halo was sliced off square at the drag box. Blur now softens the whole shape, edges and all, and the softness spreads past its edge the way a shadow does.
setup: Photonz Dev, release Next. Nothing to switch on: Blur is the third row of the Effects plus.

try.do: Draw a rectangle on a blank canvas.
With it selected, click the + on the Effects section and choose Blur.
Drag the Amount slider from 0 up to about 20 and watch the edges give way.
Untick the Blur checkbox, then tick it again.
Draw an ellipse, add a Blur, and look at the top, bottom, left and right of it.
Give the same shape a Corner Radius and an Outline, and see them go soft with it.
Drop in a screenshot, select it, and add a Blur to that instead.

evaluate: At the default 8 pt, is the softening obvious enough that you can tell the effect landed?
The halo now spills outside the selection handles. Does the shape read as smaller than its box, or does that feel like a shadow does?
The blur softens the outline and the rounded corner along with the fill. Is that what you wanted, or should a border stay crisp over a blurred fill?
Blurring a screenshot softens the picture but holds its edge, so there is no pale rim at the canvas edge. Is holding the edge right for a photo, or should a photo fade out like a shape does?
Does the slider range of 0 to 50 pt cover what you would reach for, or is the useful part squeezed into the first third?
rough: Photos are deliberately treated differently from drawn things. A shape, a label or a group fades into the clear space around it; a screenshot is blurred with its own edge held, the way a photo editor does it, because fading a full-canvas capture would leave a pale rim round the whole picture. If you would rather have one rule for everything, say so and it becomes one line.

Blur now runs after the corner radius and the border rather than before them, so a bordered box softens as one object instead of keeping a razor-sharp ring round a fuzzy fill. That is a change to how an existing blurred-and-bordered layer looks.
The shadow of a blurred layer is now cast from the blurred silhouette, so it is softer and wider than it used to be. That looks right to me, but it is a change worth an eye.
The selection handles still hug the crisp box, not the halo. That is on purpose: you resize the shape, not its glow.
The screenshots here are real window captures from the probe app, not offscreen renders.
